camaraderie

kah-muh-RAH-duh-ree -- five syllables, stress on the middle syllable, RAH. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Camaraderie is mutual trust and friendship.

A cheerful camaraderie filled the kitchen as the cousins raced to finish the holiday cooking.

Example

After three weeks of hauling gear, sharing tents, and pulling each other up the last ridge, the strangers from the first day have built a real camaraderie, trading inside jokes and finishing each other's sentences.

Camaraderie is the mutual trust and easy friendship that grows among people who share effort and time -- the warmth of comrades, not just casual acquaintance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

comradeship: Comradeship is the closeness of trusted companions who stand side by side, and it leans on loyalty -- soldiers and shipmates earn comradeship. Camaraderie names the same bond from its lighter surface: the jokes, the ease, and the good spirits a group of comrades shares.

solidarity: Solidarity is unity of feeling and purpose -- a group standing together for a cause, arms locked at the rally. Camaraderie is warmth rather than purpose: the easy friendship of people who have shared effort, whether or not they are standing up for anything.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hostility: unfriendly opposition

estrangement: the state of having grown apart

Where it sits · how hard-won and close the bond is — fellowship → camaraderie → brotherhood

fellowship vs. camaraderie: Fellowship is broader and cooler than camaraderie -- a club offers fellowship to anyone who joins, while camaraderie must be earned through shared effort: the warmth of people who have been through something together.

brotherhood vs. camaraderie: Brotherhood goes further than camaraderie: camaraderie is the earned warmth of teammates, while brotherhood binds a group so deeply that its members treat one another as family -- a loyalty meant to last a lifetime.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — camarad-

root — camarad-: chamber-mate, comrade (French camarade, from Spanish camarada, from Latin camera 'room, chamber')

suffix — -erie

suffix — -erie: state or quality of (French -erie)

Put it together

Put it together: Camaraderie is French, from camarade, 'comrade' -- originally Spanish camarada, 'chamber-mate': soldiers who slept in the same room. The word still carries that barracks warmth: camaraderie is the trust of people who share quarters, work, and risk.

Use the root in a new word: comrade

Use the root in a new word: comrade: A faded photograph of his old comrades hangs above the sailor's workbench.

Word Choice

Camaraderie grows among teams, crews, casts, and classmates -- people bound by shared effort, always on the same side. Don't confuse it with a truce: a truce merely pauses a conflict between opponents, while camaraderie is ongoing warmth among allies. Teams have camaraderie; rivals sign truces.
